title: Why Has the Monthly Cost of Buying a New Home Risen So Much?
text:
Buying a home has become considerably more difficult for many U.S. households in recent years. New home prices increased rapidly during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, while mortgage rates later rose to levels not seen in more than a decade. Looking at either factor alone, however, does not fully capture the change in the cost of homeownership.
For most buyers, the purchase price of a home is only part of the story. Because homes are typically financed with mortgages, the interest rate also determines how expensive a home is on a monthly basis. A higher home price increases the amount that must be borrowed, while a higher mortgage rate increases the cost of financing that loan.
This post asks:

How have changes in U.S. new-home prices and mortgage rates affected the monthly cost of buying a new home since 2015?

To answer this question, I examine changes in median home prices and 30-year fixed mortgage rates, and then combine them to estimate the monthly cost of purchasing a median-priced home.

title: Why Has the Monthly Cost of Buying a New Home Risen So Much?
text:
Buying a home has become considerably more difficult for many U.S. households in recent years. New home prices increased rapidly during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, while mortgage rates later rose to levels not seen in more than a decade. Looking at either factor alone, however, does not fully capture the change in the cost of homeownership.
For most buyers, the purchase price of a home is only part of the story. Because homes are typically financed with mortgages, the interest rate also determines how expensive a home is on a monthly basis. A higher home price increases the amount that must be borrowed, while a higher mortgage rate increases the cost of financing that loan.
This post asks:

How have changes in U.S. new-home prices and mortgage rates affected the monthly cost of buying a new home since 2015?

To answer this question, I examine changes in median home prices and 30-year fixed mortgage rates, and then combine them to estimate the monthly cost of purchasing a median-priced home.

title: Why Has the Monthly Cost of Buying a New Home Risen So Much?
text:
Data
I use two publicly available data series from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED):

Median Sales Price of New Houses Sold for the United States (MSPUS)
30-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage Average in the United States (MORTGAGE30US)

Both datasets are downloaded directly from FRED using URLs, making the analysis reproducible without manually downloading or updating data files.


Code
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Median sales price of houses sold in the United States
home = pd.read_csv(
    "https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=MSPUS"
)

# 30-year fixed mortgage rate
mortgage = pd.read_csv(
    "https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=MORTGAGE30US"
)

# Rename the date column
home = home.rename(columns={"observation_date": "DATE"})
mortgage = mortgage.rename(columns={"observation_date": "DATE"})

# Convert dates
home["DATE"] = pd.to_datetime(home["DATE"])
mortgage["DATE"] = pd.to_datetime(mortgage["DATE"])

# Convert values to numeric
home["MSPUS"] = pd.to_numeric(home["MSPUS"], errors="coerce")
mortgage["MORTGAGE30US"] = pd.to_numeric(
    mortgage["MORTGAGE30US"],
    errors="coerce"
)

# Keep observations from 2015 onward
home = home[home["DATE"] >= "2015-01-01"].copy()
mortgage = mortgage[mortgage["DATE"] >= "2015-01-01"].copy()

title: Why Has the Monthly Cost of Buying a New Home Risen So Much?
text:
Home Prices Rose Sharply After 2020
The first part of the cost story is the price of the home itself. Figure 1 shows the median sales price of houses sold in the United States since 2015.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))

ax.plot(
    home["DATE"],
    home["MSPUS"] / 1000,
    linewidth=2
)

ax.set_xlabel("")
ax.set_ylabel("Thousands of dollars")
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 1: Median Sales Price of U.S. New Homes, 2015–2026





From 2015 through 2019, median U.S. home prices increased gradually, rising from about $289,000 in early 2015 to a little above $320,000 before the pandemic. After a brief dip in 2020, prices began to rise much more quickly. By 2022, the median sales price had exceeded $440,000, which is more than 50 percent higher than its 2015 level.
Although home prices declined somewhat after their peak, they remained around $410,000 in 2026, still far above pre-pandemic levels. This means that even before considering interest rates, a typical homebuyer in recent years has had to finance a substantially larger loan than a buyer in the mid-2010s.

title: Why Has the Monthly Cost of Buying a New Home Risen So Much?
section: Mortgage Rates Tell the Other Half of the Story
text:
Mortgage Rates Tell the Other Half of the Story
Home prices are only one part of the cost of purchasing a home. Most households do not pay the full purchase price upfront, so the mortgage interest rate is also crucial. Figure 2 shows how the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate changed over the same period.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))

ax.plot(
    mortgage["DATE"],
    mortgage["MORTGAGE30US"],
    linewidth=2
)

ax.set_xlabel("")
ax.set_ylabel("Percent")
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 2: 30-Year Fixed Mortgage Rate in the U.S., 2015–2026





Mortgage rates followed a very different pattern from home prices. From 2015 through 2019, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate generally fluctuated between about 3.5 and 5 percent. Rates then fell sharply during the pandemic, reaching below 3 percent in 2021.
Beginning in 2022, however, mortgage rates increased rapidly. By late 2023, the average rate approached 8 percent, and although rates later declined somewhat, they remained well above their pre-pandemic levels.
This matters because a higher mortgage rate increases the monthly payment required for the same loan amount. In other words, recent buyers have faced not only higher home prices, but also much more expensive financing.

title: Why Has the Monthly Cost of Buying a New Home Risen So Much?
section: Combining Home Prices and Mortgage Rates
text:
Combining Home Prices and Mortgage Rates
To measure the combined effect of higher home prices and borrowing costs, I estimate the monthly cost of purchasing the median-priced home.

Assumptions and Calculation
I assume a 20 percent down payment and a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. Because the home-price data are quarterly while mortgage rates are weekly, I use the average mortgage rate within each quarter.
For the broader monthly-cost estimate, I also use illustrative annual costs equal to 1 percent of the home value for property taxes and 0.5 percent for homeowners insurance. These assumptions are intended to provide a consistent national benchmark; actual taxes and insurance costs vary substantially across locations and households.
For a loan amount (L), monthly interest rate (r), and (n) monthly payments, the mortgage payment is:
\[
M = L \frac{r(1+r)^n}{(1+r)^n - 1}
\]


Code
# Convert weekly mortgage rates to quarterly averages

mortgage_q = (
    mortgage
    .set_index("DATE")
    .resample("QS")["MORTGAGE30US"]
    .mean()
    .reset_index()
)

# Merge home prices with quarterly mortgage rates
housing = pd.merge(
    home,
    mortgage_q,
    on="DATE",
    how="inner"
)

# Mortgage assumptions
down_payment_rate = 0.20
property_tax_rate = 0.01
insurance_rate = 0.005

# Loan amount after 20% down payment
housing["loan_amount"] = (
    housing["MSPUS"] * (1 - down_payment_rate)
)

# Monthly interest rate
housing["monthly_rate"] = (
    housing["MORTGAGE30US"] / 100 / 12
)

# Number of monthly payments in a 30-year mortgage
n = 30 * 12

# Monthly mortgage principal + interest
housing["monthly_payment"] = (
    housing["loan_amount"]
    * (
        housing["monthly_rate"]
        * (1 + housing["monthly_rate"]) ** n
    )
    / (
        (1 + housing["monthly_rate"]) ** n - 1
    )
)

# Monthly property tax
housing["property_tax"] = (
    housing["MSPUS"] * property_tax_rate / 12
)

# Monthly homeowners insurance
housing["insurance"] = (
    housing["MSPUS"] * insurance_rate / 12
)

# Total monthly cost excluding HOA
housing["monthly_cost_no_hoa"] = (
    housing["monthly_payment"]
    + housing["property_tax"]
    + housing["insurance"]
)

title: Why Has the Monthly Cost of Buying a New Home Risen So Much?
section: The Combined Monthly Cost of Buying a New Home
text:
The Combined Monthly Cost of Buying a New Home
To see how these changes translate into a household’s monthly budget, I combine home prices and mortgage rates and estimate the monthly cost of purchasing the median-priced home.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))

ax.plot(
    housing["DATE"],
    housing["monthly_payment"],
    linewidth=2,
    label="Mortgage principal + interest"
)

ax.plot(
    housing["DATE"],
    housing["monthly_cost_no_hoa"],
    linewidth=2,
    label="Including property tax + insurance"
)


ax.set_xlabel("")
ax.set_ylabel("Monthly cost ($)")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()



peak = housing.loc[
    housing["monthly_cost_no_hoa"].idxmax()
]








Figure 3: Estimated Monthly Cost of Buying a Median-Priced U.S. New Home





As shown in Figure 3, the combined measure reveals a much sharper increase in monthly purchasing costs than home prices alone. Estimated monthly housing costs increased rapidly after 2021 as buyers faced both high home prices and sharply higher mortgage rates.
Under the assumptions used here, the estimated monthly cost of purchasing the median-priced U.S. home peaked at about $2,871 per month in the third quarter of 2023. This includes mortgage principal and interest, estimated property taxes, and homeowners insurance.
The gap between the two lines also shows that mortgage payments alone understate the monthly cost of homeownership. Property taxes and insurance add several hundred dollars per month, and these costs also rise as home values increase.


Code
start = housing.iloc[0]
latest = housing.iloc[-1]

increase_pct = (
    latest["monthly_cost_no_hoa"]
    / start["monthly_cost_no_hoa"]
    - 1
) * 100

start_cost = f"${start['monthly_cost_no_hoa']:,.0f}"
latest_cost = f"${latest['monthly_cost_no_hoa']:,.0f}"
increase_text = f"{increase_pct:.0f} percent"
peak_cost = f"${peak['monthly_cost_no_hoa']:,.0f}"

title: Why Has the Monthly Cost of Buying a New Home Risen So Much?
text:
Takeaway
The three figures tell a consistent story. U.S. home prices rose substantially after 2020, while mortgage rates also increased sharply beginning in 2022. When these two forces are combined, the monthly cost of buying a home increased much more than either series alone would suggest.
Under the assumptions used in this analysis, the estimated monthly cost of purchasing the median-priced new U.S. home increased from about $1,429 in 2015 to $2,572 in the latest observation, an increase of approximately 80 percent. The estimated cost peaked at about $2,871 per month in the third quarter of 2023.
This shows that the increase in the monthly cost of buying a home cannot be explained by home prices alone. Higher borrowing costs have amplified the effect of already-elevated home prices, while property taxes and homeowners insurance add further costs beyond the mortgage payment itself.
The broader lesson is that the financial burden of purchasing a home is better understood by considering the monthly costs faced by buyers rather than focusing only on the sale price.

title: What Technical Skills Do Economic Consulting Firms Actually Want?
text:
Students interested in economic consulting are often told to learn a wide range of technical tools: Excel, R, Python, Stata, SQL, SAS, and sometimes more specialized software. But if recruiting season is approaching and time is limited, which skills should a student actually prioritize?
To investigate this question, I scraped current entry-level job postings from two economic consulting firms, The Brattle Group and Charles River Associates (CRA). My goal was not simply to collect job listings, but to use the postings to identify which technical skills appear consistently across firms and which seem more firm-specific.

title: What Technical Skills Do Economic Consulting Firms Actually Want?
text:
Students interested in economic consulting are often told to learn a wide range of technical tools: Excel, R, Python, Stata, SQL, SAS, and sometimes more specialized software. But if recruiting season is approaching and time is limited, which skills should a student actually prioritize?
To investigate this question, I scraped current entry-level job postings from two economic consulting firms, The Brattle Group and Charles River Associates (CRA). My goal was not simply to collect job listings, but to use the postings to identify which technical skills appear consistently across firms and which seem more firm-specific.

title: What Technical Skills Do Economic Consulting Firms Actually Want?
text:
Collecting the Data
I used the rvest package in R to collect publicly available job postings from The Brattle Group’s Greenhouse job board and Charles River Associates’ Greenhouse job board.
I used the rvest package in R to collect publicly available job postings from the firms’ Greenhouse job boards. I only accessed pages that were publicly visible and did not attempt to bypass logins, CAPTCHAs, or other access restrictions.
For Brattle, I scraped the firm’s Greenhouse job-board page to collect individual job URLs and then visited each posting. For CRA, I used two publicly available U.S. entry-level economics consulting postings hosted on its Greenhouse site.


Code
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

scrape_brattle_job <- function(url) {

  Sys.sleep(1)

  page <- read_html(url)

  tibble(
    job_title = page |> html_element("h1") |> html_text2(),
    job_url = url,
    job_description = page |> html_element("body") |> html_text2()
  )
}


I then restricted the sample to U.S. entry-level analyst and internship positions. Because the same Brattle position was sometimes posted separately for multiple cities, I removed duplicate job titles so that one job description would not receive more weight simply because it was offered in several locations.
The final sample contained eight unique U.S. entry-level job types: six from Brattle and two from CRA.

title: What Technical Skills Do Economic Consulting Firms Actually Want?
text:
Which Skills Appear Most Often?
I searched each job description for eight technical skills: Excel, R, Python, Stata, SQL, SAS, VBA, and GAMS. Each skill was coded as either present or absent in a posting.

The first result is striking. Excel, R, Python, and Stata appeared in all eight job types in the sample. SAS and VBA appeared in six of the eight, while SQL and GAMS appeared in only two.
This suggests that the most useful preparation is not choosing between R and Python. At least in these postings, employers frequently mention both, alongside Stata and Excel. A student preparing for entry-level economic consulting would therefore benefit from being comfortable moving between spreadsheet analysis, statistical software, and general-purpose programming.

title: What Technical Skills Do Economic Consulting Firms Actually Want?
section: Do Firms Ask for the Same Skills?
text:
Do Firms Ask for the Same Skills?
The overall percentages hide an important difference between firms.

Both Brattle and CRA consistently mentioned Excel, R, Python, and Stata, suggesting that these four tools form a common technical core in this sample.
The more specialized skills differed substantially. All six Brattle job types mentioned VBA, while neither CRA posting did. GAMS appeared in some Brattle roles but neither CRA role. In contrast, both CRA job types mentioned SQL, while none of the six Brattle job types did. SAS appeared in both firms, although more consistently at CRA.
This distinction matters because a simple industry-wide ranking can hide differences in how individual firms work.

title: What Technical Skills Do Economic Consulting Firms Actually Want?
section: What Should a Student Learn First?
text:
What Should a Student Learn First?
Based on these postings, I would divide preparation into two stages.
First, prioritize Excel, R, Python, and Stata. They were the only four skills mentioned across every job type in the sample, making them the strongest candidates for broadly transferable preparation.
Second, tailor additional skills to the firms being targeted. For example, VBA and GAMS may be especially useful for some Brattle roles, while SQL appears more relevant in the CRA postings examined here.
There are important limitations. This is a small sample of eight unique job types from only two firms, and job postings change over time. The results therefore describe these postings rather than the entire economic consulting industry.

title: What Technical Skills Do Economic Consulting Firms Actually Want?
text:
Takeaway
Web scraping turns scattered job descriptions into structured information that can support a practical decision. In this sample, the clearest pattern is a shared core of Excel, R, Python, and Stata, followed by more firm-specific tools such as SAS, VBA, SQL, and GAMS.
For a student with limited preparation time, the evidence from these postings suggests building the common core first and then using current postings from target firms to decide which specialized tools to learn next.

title: What Is a P-Value, Really?
text:
Suppose a researcher runs an experiment and reports a p-value of 0.03. What does that number actually mean?
A common interpretation is that there is only a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true. This sounds reasonable, but it is incorrect.
The p-value is one of the most widely used ideas in statistics, but also one of the most frequently misunderstood. The main reason is that it answers a slightly different question from the one people naturally want to ask.

title: What Is a P-Value, Really?
text:
Suppose a researcher runs an experiment and reports a p-value of 0.03. What does that number actually mean?
A common interpretation is that there is only a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true. This sounds reasonable, but it is incorrect.
The p-value is one of the most widely used ideas in statistics, but also one of the most frequently misunderstood. The main reason is that it answers a slightly different question from the one people naturally want to ask.

title: What Is a P-Value, Really?
text:
A Simple Coin Example
Imagine that someone claims a coin is fair. If the coin is truly fair, the probability of getting heads is
\[
H_0: p = 0.5
\] Now suppose we flip the coin 20 times and observe 16 heads.
Getting 16 heads out of 20 seems unusual for a fair coin. The p-value gives us a way to measure exactly how unusual this result is.
In this case, the p-value asks:

If the coin really were fair, what is the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as 16 heads out of 20?

For a two-sided test, this probability is about 0.012, or 1.2%.
So the data would be fairly unusual if the coin were actually fair.

title: What Is a P-Value, Really?
section: What the P-Value Does — and Does Not — Mean
text:
What the P-Value Does — and Does Not — Mean
The easiest way to understand a p-value is to pay attention to the direction of the probability.
A p-value measures
\[
P(\text{data at least as extreme as observed} \mid H_0).
\]
In words, we assume the null hypothesis is true and then ask how surprising the observed data would be.
But this is not the same as
\[
P(H_0 \mid \text{data}),
\]
which would mean the probability that the null hypothesis is true given the data.
This difference is subtle but important. A p-value of 0.03 does not mean that there is a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true. It means that, if the null hypothesis were true, results at least as extreme as the one we observed would occur about 3% of the time.

title: What Is a P-Value, Really?
text:
A Useful Analogy: Medical Testing
Consider a medical test for a rare disease.
Suppose the test is very accurate, and only 1% of healthy people receive a positive result. In probability notation, this is
\[
P(\text{positive} \mid \text{healthy}) = 0.01.
\]
Now imagine that your test comes back positive.
Can we conclude that there is only a 1% chance that you are healthy?
No.
What we actually want to know is
\[
P(\text{healthy} \mid \text{positive}),
\]
which is a different probability.
To calculate that probability, we would also need other information, such as how common the disease is in the population.
The same logic applies to p-values. A small probability of observing the data under the null hypothesis does not automatically tell us the probability that the null hypothesis itself is true.

title: What Is a P-Value, Really?
section: What Does a Small P-Value Tell Us?
text:
What Does a Small P-Value Tell Us?
Suppose a statistical test gives us
\[
p = 0.03.
\]
This means that, if the null hypothesis were true, results at least as extreme as the one we observed would occur about 3% of the time.
Because such a result would be relatively unusual under the null hypothesis, the data provide evidence against (H_0).
Researchers often compare the p-value with a significance level such as
\[
\alpha = 0.05.
\]
If the p-value is smaller than 0.05, the result is often called statistically significant, and researchers may reject the null hypothesis.
Importantly, statistical significance is evidence against the null hypothesis, not a statement about the probability that either hypothesis is true.

title: What Is a P-Value, Really?
text:
Takeaway
A p-value does not tell us the probability that a hypothesis is true. Instead, it tells us how unusual our data would be if the null hypothesis were true.
The easiest way to remember it is:

Assume the null hypothesis is true. How surprising is the data?

Once this direction of probability is clear, p-values become much less mysterious.

title: Education and Labor Market Outcomes in the U.S.
text:
How do labor market outcomes differ across education groups in the United States? Education is closely connected to workers’ opportunities in the labor market, so differences in unemployment and labor force participation can help show which groups are more exposed to weak labor market conditions.
This post uses IPUMS CPS Basic Monthly Survey microdata to compare adults ages 25–64 across four education groups. I use July samples from 2015 to 2026 and calculate population statistics using the CPS final person weight, WTFINL.
I restrict the sample to ages 25–64 to focus on working-age adults who have largely completed their education. I group educational attainment into four categories: high school or less, some college or an associate degree, a bachelor’s degree, and a graduate degree. The unemployment rate is calculated among people in the labor force, while the labor force participation rate measures the share of the working-age population that is either employed or actively looking for work.

title: Education and Labor Market Outcomes in the U.S.
text:
How do labor market outcomes differ across education groups in the United States? Education is closely connected to workers’ opportunities in the labor market, so differences in unemployment and labor force participation can help show which groups are more exposed to weak labor market conditions.
This post uses IPUMS CPS Basic Monthly Survey microdata to compare adults ages 25–64 across four education groups. I use July samples from 2015 to 2026 and calculate population statistics using the CPS final person weight, WTFINL.
I restrict the sample to ages 25–64 to focus on working-age adults who have largely completed their education. I group educational attainment into four categories: high school or less, some college or an associate degree, a bachelor’s degree, and a graduate degree. The unemployment rate is calculated among people in the labor force, while the labor force participation rate measures the share of the working-age population that is either employed or actively looking for work.

title: Education and Labor Market Outcomes in the U.S.
text:
Unemployment by Education
The first figure compares unemployment rates across education groups in July 2026.









In July 2026, unemployment was highest among adults with a high school education or less, at 4.4%, and lowest among those with graduate degrees, at 2.6%. The differences are not extremely large in absolute terms, but the ordering is clear: unemployment generally falls as educational attainment rises. This pattern is consistent with more educated workers having stronger attachment to employment, although the descriptive data alone cannot establish a causal effect of education.

title: Education and Labor Market Outcomes in the U.S.
text:
Changes Over Time
Looking across years shows whether the education gap observed in 2026 is a persistent pattern or only a feature of one year.









The education gap also persists over time. All four groups experienced a sharp increase in unemployment in July 2020, during the COVID-19 labor market disruption. The rise was especially pronounced among adults with a high school education or less and those with some college education. Unemployment declined substantially afterward, but the lower-education groups generally continued to have higher rates.

title: Education and Labor Market Outcomes in the U.S.
text:
Labor Force Participation
Education is also associated with labor force participation. In 2026, participation increased steadily with educational attainment, ranging from about 71% among adults with a high school education or less to nearly 88% among those with graduate degrees.









The differences in labor force participation are also substantial. This suggests that education is related not only to employment outcomes among labor-force participants, but also to whether working-age adults participate in the labor market at all.

title: Education and Labor Market Outcomes in the U.S.
text:
Conclusion
The CPS data show a consistent relationship between education and labor market outcomes. Adults with more education generally have lower unemployment and higher labor force participation. These are descriptive patterns and should not be interpreted as causal effects of education.

title: The Geography of Income in Philadelphia
text:
Income inequality is not only about differences between individuals. It also has an important geographic dimension. Within the same city, households in different neighborhoods may experience very different economic conditions.
In this post, I explore the geographic distribution of median household income across Philadelphia using data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey (ACS). By mapping income at the census tract level, I examine where higher- and lower-income areas are concentrated and what these patterns suggest about spatial inequality.

title: The Geography of Income in Philadelphia
text:
Income inequality is not only about differences between individuals. It also has an important geographic dimension. Within the same city, households in different neighborhoods may experience very different economic conditions.
In this post, I explore the geographic distribution of median household income across Philadelphia using data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey (ACS). By mapping income at the census tract level, I examine where higher- and lower-income areas are concentrated and what these patterns suggest about spatial inequality.

title: The Geography of Income in Philadelphia
text:
Data and Methods
This analysis uses data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-Year Estimates, covering the period from 2020 to 2024. The data were obtained using the tidycensus package in R.
The main variable is median household income (B19013_001), measured in 2024 inflation-adjusted dollars. I focus on census tracts within Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania. Census tracts are relatively small geographic areas that allow us to examine income differences within the city.
To prepare the data, I removed census tracts with missing or invalid income estimates. I then combined the income information with geographic boundaries provided by the Census Bureau.
For visualization, I used the sf and ggplot2 packages to create a choropleth map. Each census tract is shaded according to its median household income, with lighter yellow representing lower incomes and darker red representing higher incomes.
Because ACS figures are survey estimates, they are subject to sampling uncertainty. Furthermore, census tract boundaries do not necessarily correspond to commonly recognized neighborhood boundaries.

title: The Geography of Income in Philadelphia
text:
Mapping Household Income
The map below illustrates the geographic distribution of median household income across Philadelphia’s census tracts.






Figure 1: Median household income across Philadelphia census tracts. Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 2024 5-Year Estimates.



The map reveals substantial geographic variation in household income across Philadelphia. Higher-income census tracts appear in several clusters, particularly in parts of northwestern Philadelphia. Meanwhile, many other areas have considerably lower median household incomes.
These differences suggest that income inequality in Philadelphia has a strong spatial dimension. Rather than being evenly distributed throughout the city, higher- and lower-income households appear to be concentrated in particular geographic areas.
However, the map represents median household income at the census tract level, not the income of individual residents. It also does not establish why these geographic differences exist.

title: The Geography of Income in Philadelphia
text:
Discussion
The income data reveal substantial economic differences across Philadelphia’s 375 census tracts. The median of tract-level median household incomes is approximately $62,083, while the average is $68,707. The 25th percentile is $43,529, compared with $88,647 at the 75th percentile. This means that the median household income in a tract at the 75th percentile is approximately twice that of a tract at the 25th percentile.
The differences become even more pronounced when comparing the extremes. The lowest observed tract median household income is $17,875, while the highest is $227,656. Although these extreme values may not represent typical neighborhoods, they illustrate the wide variation in local economic conditions within Philadelphia.
The map adds an important geographic perspective to these statistics. Higher-income areas appear concentrated in certain parts of the city, including portions of northwestern Philadelphia, while lower-income tracts are distributed across many other areas. These patterns suggest that income differences are not randomly scattered across the city.
Several factors could contribute to these geographic differences, including housing costs, historical development, access to employment opportunities, and residential sorting. However, this descriptive analysis cannot establish which factors cause the observed patterns.
It is also important to recognize that census tract median income does not represent every household within a tract. Furthermore, the statistics summarize tracts rather than individual households, and ACS estimates are subject to sampling uncertainty.

title: The Geography of Income in Philadelphia
text:
Conclusion
This analysis highlights the geographic dimension of income inequality in Philadelphia. Using ACS data and GIS visualization, I find substantial differences in median household income across the city’s census tracts.
The comparison between the 25th and 75th percentiles suggests that income differences are not limited to a few extreme observations. The map further illustrates how these differences vary across geographic areas.
The main takeaway is that understanding urban economic inequality requires attention not only to income levels but also to where households live. Geographic visualization provides a useful starting point for identifying patterns that may motivate further research into housing affordability, neighborhood development, and economic opportunity.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text: Tutorial data: This post uses simulated longitudinal family data, not PSID or observed U.S. income data. All conclusions concern the simulated example.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
1. Introduction: Why study intergenerational mobility?
How closely tied are the future earnings of a child to the earnings of its parents? Understanding intergenerational economic mobility depends on this topic.
Economists frequently assess this link using the intergenerational income elasticity (IGE). The larger the IGE, the stronger the relationship between parent and child income and thus the smaller the intergenerational mobility.
In this lesson, we’ll be matching parents and children in a simulated longitudinal dataset using Python and SQL. We will next estimate IGE using single year and multi-year average income. Finally, we will go over the implications of income measurement and life-cycle bias on our estimates.
At the end of this session you will know how to use SQL to join family information, build income measures, and analyse estimates of intergenerational income mobility.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
2. Understanding the Data
Before matching parents and children, we need to understand how the data are organized.
For this tutorial, we use a simulated longitudinal dataset containing 1,200 families, with one parent and one child in each family. Each individual has income observations from 2010 to 2019, giving us 2,400 individuals and 24,000 person-year records.
The dataset is organized into two tables:

individuals.csv: Contains individual identifiers (person_id), family identifiers (family_id), and each person’s role (parent or child).
earnings.csv: Contains annual income observations for each individual, identified by person_id and year.

The person_id uniquely identifies each individual, while the family_id connects parents and children who belong to the same family. Since income observations are stored separately, we need SQL to combine the relevant information.
For example, we can use the following Python code to load the datasets:
import pandas as pd

individuals = pd.read_csv("data/individuals.csv")
earnings = pd.read_csv("data/earnings.csv")

print(individuals.head())
print(earnings.head())
The first table describes who each person is and which family they belong to, while the second describes how their income changes over time.
This separation is common in longitudinal datasets and makes SQL particularly useful for combining information across individuals and years.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
section: 3. Matching Parents and Children Using SQL
text:
3. Matching Parents and Children Using SQL
Now that we understand the data structure, we can use SQL to connect parents and children.
Python provides a built-in library called sqlite3, which allows us to execute SQL queries directly within Python.

Step 1: Create a SQLite Database
First, we load our datasets into an in-memory SQLite database.
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")

individuals.to_sql("individuals", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")
earnings.to_sql("earnings", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")
The :memory: option creates a temporary database. The to_sql() function converts our pandas DataFrames into SQL tables.


Step 2: Explore the Data with SELECT
The SELECT statement allows us to choose specific columns from a table.
query = """
SELECT person_id, family_id, role
FROM individuals
LIMIT 6;
"""

print(pd.read_sql_query(query, conn))
Here, SELECT specifies the columns we want, FROM identifies the table, and LIMIT restricts the output to six rows.


Step 3: Match Parents and Children Using JOIN
Next, we connect parents and children using their shared family_id.
query = """
SELECT
    p.person_id AS parent_id,
    c.person_id AS child_id,
    p.family_id
FROM individuals AS p
JOIN individuals AS c
    ON c.parent_id = p.person_id
    AND c.family_id = p.family_id
WHERE p.role = 'parent'
  AND c.role = 'child';
"""

matched = pd.read_sql_query(query, conn)

print(matched.head())
print("Matched parent-child pairs:", len(matched))
This is a self-join, meaning that we join a table with itself.
We use p to represent parents and c to represent children. The JOIN operation connects each child’s parent_id to the corresponding parent’s person_id, while family_id verifies that both individuals belong to the same family. The WHERE clause ensures that each match contains one parent and one child.
In our simulated dataset, this produces 1,200 matched parent–child pairs.


Step 4: Calculate Average Income Using GROUP BY
After identifying family relationships, we can summarize annual income for each individual.
query = """
SELECT
    person_id,
    AVG(income) AS average_income,
    COUNT(*) AS years_observed
FROM earnings
GROUP BY person_id;
"""

average_income = pd.read_sql_query(query, conn)

print(average_income.head())
The GROUP BY statement combines observations belonging to the same person.
The aggregation functions AVG() and COUNT() calculate each person’s average annual income and number of observed years, respectively.
These SQL processes, in sum, allow us to convert distinct person and income data into information useful for the analysis of intergenerational mobility.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
4. Constructing Income Measures
To estimate the IGE, we need income measures for both parents and children. We compare income from 2010 with average income from 2010–2019.
The following SQL query combines our matched pairs with annual earnings and calculates both measures.
query = """
SELECT
    m.parent_id,
    m.child_id,
    AVG(CASE WHEN p.year = 2010 THEN p.income END)
        AS parent_single,
    AVG(CASE WHEN c.year = 2010 THEN c.income END)
        AS child_single,
    AVG(CASE
    WHEN p.year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2019
    THEN p.income
END) AS parent_average,

AVG(CASE
    WHEN c.year BETWEEN 2010 AND 2019
    THEN c.income
END) AS child_average
FROM matched AS m
JOIN earnings AS p
    ON m.parent_id = p.person_id
JOIN earnings AS c
    ON m.child_id = c.person_id
    AND p.year = c.year
GROUP BY m.parent_id, m.child_id;
"""

matched.to_sql("matched", conn, index=False, if_exists="replace")

income_data = pd.read_sql_query(query, conn)
print(income_data.head())
CASE WHEN selects income from 2010, while AVG() calculates average income over the specified 2010–2019 period. Matching the years prevents duplicate combinations of annual observations.
Single-year income may contain temporary fluctuations, such as bonuses or unemployment. Averaging several years reduces the influence of these fluctuations and may better approximate long-run economic status.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
5. Estimating the Intergenerational Income Elasticity
We estimate the IGE using a log-log regression:
\[
\ln(Y_{\text{child}}) = \alpha + \beta \ln(Y_{\text{parent}}) + \varepsilon
\]
Here, \(\beta\) measures the association between parental and child income. A higher IGE indicates stronger income persistence across generations.
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm

def estimate_ige(data, parent_col, child_col):
    df = data[[parent_col, child_col]].dropna()
    df = df[(df[parent_col] > 0) & (df[child_col] > 0)]

    X = sm.add_constant(np.log(df[parent_col]))
    y = np.log(df[child_col])

    model = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()
    return model.params.iloc[1]

ige_single = estimate_ige(
    income_data, "parent_single", "child_single"
)

ige_average = estimate_ige(
    income_data, "parent_average", "child_average"
)

print(f"Single-year IGE: {ige_single:.5f}")
print(f"Ten-year average IGE: {ige_average:.5f}")
Our simulated results are:



Income measure
Estimated IGE




Single-year income (2010)
0.194


Ten-year average income (2010–2019)
0.385



The larger estimate from the averaged income shows that transient income changes could attenuate the observed intergenerational association when just one year is studied. These conclusions are based on simulated data, not actual income mobility in the US.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
6. Understanding Life-Cycle Bias
Life-cycle bias arises when income at a certain age is not a good proxy for the long-run economic position of the individual.
For example, younger workers may have lower wages while they are in school or acquiring experience, whereas older workers may have more steady incomes.
We can see this by calculating the IGE at different ages of the children.









The calculated IGE of the 22-year-old is about 0.194 in magnitude, substantially below than the stimulated long-run value of 0.43. It normally increased with the age of children, reaching around 0.44 at age 31.
This trend suggests the possibility of life-cycle bias, i.e., income observed early in a worker’s career may be unrepresentative of long-run earning capabilities. Averaging income across several years smoothes out transitory changes, and the estimate for the IGE is 0.385, closer to the estimated long-run value. However, averaging does not automatically eliminate life-cycle bias.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
7. Conclusion
In this lesson we used Python and SQL to match 1,200 parent-child pairings and estimate inter-generational income elasticity.
Our simulated results indicate that the IGE rises from 0.194 with single-year income to 0.385 with ten-year average income. This disparity underscores the significance of income assessment on intergenerational mobility results.
The essential lesson is the need of precise matching of people as well as exact measurement of income. SQL gives a consistent technique to build family bonds and multi-year income metrics assist to iron out short-term variations. Researchers should also be mindful of life-cycle impacts when assessing intergenerational income estimates.

title: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
8. Reproducing This Tutorial
All data and results in this tutorial can be reproduced using the Python scripts in the accompanying GitHub repository.
First, install the required Python packages:
pip install -r requirements.txt
Next, generate the simulated longitudinal dataset:
python scripts/generate_data.py
Finally, run the SQL matching and IGE analysis:
python scripts/analyze.py
The first script generates the individual and annual income records. The second matches parents and children using SQL, estimates the IGE, and saves the resulting tables and visualizations.
Because the data are simulated, the findings should be interpreted as a demonstration of the methodology rather than evidence about actual intergenerational mobility in the United States.
See the GitHub project README for commands to generate all data, results and figures from code.
